title: Longshore work and carnival parades; Blanche as paymaster
summary: Laine worked on the river through his brother-in-law, who let him off for music jobs; Blanche paid the band.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Were you still a pretty young... Was that before you started playing for money? Oh, no. It was after. It was after you started playing for money that you left school? Yeah. I see. When did you start making enough money in music to make a living? When did you first start making enough money out of music to make a living? When did I first start? No. When did you first start making good money? When did you first start making good money so you could support yourself out of music?
Well, I'll tell you. I didn't only play music, but I worked on the river.

With my brother-in-law. You understand? What kind of work? Longshore. Longshore. My brother-in-law was a boss out there. And whenever I had a job, like tonight, I'd have a job, I'd get off at 12 o'clock today. That's it. That's it, brother? He'd leave me off. That's it, brother? Uh-huh. He'd say, hey, so too. What was his name?
Okay. Smith. He was for the Puerto Rico Steelship Company. He was superintendent.
And I'd play when I'd play them carnival parades and carnival balls. You understand? I had a pay list. It's not long. Is that right?
You used to play this ragtime at carnival balls. Is that right? They liked it, huh?

Oh, they loved it. Uh-huh. They loved it. Yeah. And they'd come down to the house and get their money. All that brothers would come down to the house and get their money. She was my paymaster. I see. When I wouldn't be there or anything, she'd handle all the business. Uh-huh. But they were all right. But when I wouldn't do it, she'd handle all the business. They'd come along there, you know, and stop. If I was there all right, here's your money.
